correctness.rationale: A two-letter projection preserving one unequal position commutes with rotation, and its separating DFA lifts to the full alphabet. Binary witnesses also give lower bounds on a larger alphabet, since other letters are never read. The inverse shift yields the same unordered pairs. For a one-symbol shift, either a last-bit recorder works or a reset and swap record the parity of trailing equal bits, whose lengths differ by one. For a two-symbol constant prefix, a reset and a 3-cycle distinguish trailing run lengths differing by two. For a mixed prefix, independent saturation from the two written triples reproduced all 12 transformations, their transitions and commuting indices 0, 4 and 10. The closed product with the recognizer for (01)* certifies the full word language, not just a finite length cutoff. Noncommuting actions differ on a selectable initial state and thus admit a distinguishing accepting set. For sharpness at n≥4, the pair 0^(n−2)10 and 0^(n−4)1000 has the same Parikh vector and ends in 0. A constant on 0 makes their actions identical; two permutation actions commute; and with a constant on 1 the trailing counts 1 and 3 act identically under any two-point permutation. This exhausts all two-state transitions. The frozen verifier and recorded output were inspected, not executed. Independent construction checks covered 8,166 one-step and 8,154 two-step distinct binary rotations for lengths 2–12, and checked all 16 two-state transition-map pairs on the lower family for 4≤n≤24. The exact theorems are about maxima, not equality of every individual separation number.

value.rationale: Nearest shifts are natural cases of the extremal conjugate-separation problem, whose prior bounds are not sharp there. The all-length three-state upper construction with a finite transition closure, paired with an all-length obstruction to two states, improves the upper bound of five and resolves the exact worst-case constant. The finite graph is useful because it certifies arbitrarily long inputs, not because of the number of small cases counted.
